set1.q: A 61-year-old man has sustained ventricular tachycardia while admitted with a severe infection and is too unwell for device implantation now. Which device can detect and shock a lethal ventricular rhythm in the meantime?
opts: Wearable defibrillator vest
Correct. A wearable (external) cardioverter defibrillator, worn as a vest, detects fatal ventricular arrhythmias and delivers a shock until an implantable device can be placed.
Ambulatory Holter monitor
A Holter monitor only records the rhythm; it cannot shock. The wearable defibrillator vest can.
Implantable loop recorder
A loop recorder only stores the rhythm. A wearable defibrillator vest detects and shocks lethal rhythms.
Transcutaneous pacing pads
Pacing pads treat slow rhythms in an emergency. The wearable defibrillator vest is the device that shocks lethal rhythms.

set1.q: A 38-year-old woman has bothersome palpitations. Her echocardiogram is normal, a 24-hour monitor shows premature ventricular contractions in 3% of beats, she has never fainted, and her electrolytes and oxygen saturation are normal. She has already stopped caffeine. Which is the first-line treatment?
opts: Amiodarone
Amiodarone is an antiarrhythmic for ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation. A beta blocker is first-line here.
Beta blocker
Correct. In low-risk patients with symptoms, a beta blocker is first-line; catheter ablation follows only if symptoms are refractory or the drug is not tolerated.
Catheter ablation
Ablation is second-line in low-risk patients, used when a beta blocker fails or is not tolerated.
Implantable defibrillator
A defibrillator prevents sudden death from lethal rhythms. Symptomatic benign premature beats start with a beta blocker.

set1.q: A 66-year-old woman collapses in a hospital hallway. The monitor shows chaotic, uncoordinated activity, and she has no pulse. Compressions have started and defibrillator pads are attached. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion
Synchronized cardioversion needs a QRS to time against. Fibrillation has none, so the shock is unsynchronized.
Amiodarone before any shock
Amiodarone is added when fibrillation persists after shocks. The first step is defibrillation as soon as possible.
Check electrolytes first
Delaying the shock for labs costs her chance of survival. Defibrillate as soon as possible.
Defibrillate now
Correct. Ventricular fibrillation is treated as cardiac arrest with cardiopulmonary resuscitation, oxygen and defibrillation (unsynchronized cardioversion) as soon as possible.

set1.q: A 58-year-old man collapses in a gym. He is unresponsive, not breathing and has no pulse. The monitor shows chaotic, irregular waves of varying size with no identifiable QRS complexes. Which rhythm is present?
opts: Asystole
Asystole is a flat line with no electrical activity. Chaotic waves mean ventricular fibrillation.
Pulseless electrical activity
Pulseless electrical activity shows an organized rhythm without a pulse. This rhythm is chaotic.
Ventricular fibrillation
Correct. Uncoordinated electrical activity with no rate, no P waves and no organized QRS, in a pulseless patient, is ventricular fibrillation.
Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia
Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia still has identifiable, if varying, QRS complexes. Chaotic waves without any QRS are fibrillation.

set1.q: A 71-year-old woman in cardiac arrest has an organized sinus rhythm on the monitor but no pulse. A team member begins to charge the defibrillator. Which statement is accurate?
opts: Defibrillate now
Defibrillation is for ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia. An organized pulseless rhythm is unshockable.
Use a synchronized shock
Shocking an already organized rhythm achieves nothing. Pulseless electrical activity is unshockable.
Start transcutaneous pacing
Pacing is for slow rhythms with a pulse. She is pulseless and needs compressions and epinephrine.
The rhythm is unshockable
Correct. Pulseless electrical activity and asystole are unshockable; chest compressions start immediately, with epinephrine and early intubation.

set1.q: A 55-year-old man is cardioverted from unstable sustained ventricular tachycardia. He is now stable in sinus rhythm, and no reversible cause is found. Which is the most appropriate plan before discharge?
opts: Implantable defibrillator
Correct. Once stabilized, most patients need an implantable cardioverter defibrillator for secondary prevention of sudden cardiac death from ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation.
Permanent pacemaker
A pacemaker treats slow conduction. After unstable ventricular tachycardia, the device needed is a defibrillator.
No further therapy
He remains at risk of sudden death; most survivors need a defibrillator for secondary prevention.
Lifelong oral magnesium
Magnesium treats torsades acutely and does not prevent sudden death. He needs an implantable defibrillator.

set1.q: A 76-year-old woman with long-standing hypertension and diabetes has two spells of lightheadedness this week. Her electrocardiogram shows regular P waves, a constant PR interval of 0.16 seconds in the conducted beats, and occasional P waves with no QRS complex after them, with no lengthening of the PR beforehand. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Complete heart block
In complete block no P wave conducts and the P waves and QRS complexes are unrelated. Here most P waves conduct at a fixed PR.
Mobitz type II block
Correct. A constant PR interval with random dropped QRS complexes is Mobitz type II block; acquired His-Purkinje disease from age, hypertension and diabetes is its most common cause.
Mobitz type I block
Mobitz type I lengthens the PR before each dropped beat. Here the PR stays constant, which marks Mobitz type II.
First-degree block
First-degree block has a long PR and never drops a beat. Here the PR is normal and some P waves fail to conduct.

set1.q: A 59-year-old woman with acute chest pain develops polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (QRS complexes that vary in shape) with a normal QT and is defibrillated back to sinus rhythm. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Urgent coronary angiography

Correct. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia without a prolonged QT is most commonly due to acute ischemia, so defibrillation is followed by urgent coronary angiography with possible revascularization.
Outpatient stress test
A stress test weeks later delays treatment of acute ischemia. Urgent coronary angiography is the next step.
Pericardiocentesis
Pericardiocentesis drains a tamponade, which nothing here suggests. Urgent coronary angiography is next.
Catheter ablation
Ablation is not the urgent step. Ischemia-driven polymorphic ventricular tachycardia needs coronary angiography.

set1.q: A 34-year-old woman has an electrocardiogram before a sports tryout. The QRS is 0.14 seconds, with an rsR' pattern (a small upward wave, a dip, then a taller second upward wave) in V1 to V3 and a slurred S wave in leads I and aVL. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Accessory pathway
An accessory pathway gives a short PR and a slurred QRS upstroke (a delta wave), not rsR' in the right precordial leads.
Ventricular tachycardia
Ventricular tachycardia is a fast wide rhythm without P waves. A routine tracing with rsR' in V1 is right bundle branch block.
Right bundle branch block
Correct. A QRS over 0.12 seconds with rsR' (bunny ears) in V1 to V3 and a slurred S wave in I and aVL is right bundle branch block.
Left bundle branch block
Left bundle branch block gives a dominant S wave in V1 and absent Q waves in the lateral leads, not rsR' in V1.

set1.q: A 24-year-old marathon runner has an electrocardiogram at a sports physical. He has no symptoms. The PR interval grows longer with each beat until one P wave is not followed by a QRS complex, and then the cycle repeats. The QRS complexes are narrow. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: First-degree block
First-degree block has a long but constant PR and never drops a beat. Here a P wave fails to conduct after the PR lengthens.
Complete heart block
Complete block has no relationship between P waves and QRS complexes. Here the PR changes in an orderly pattern tied to the drop.
Mobitz type I block
Correct. A PR interval that progressively lengthens until a QRS drops, in a repeating pattern, is Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) block; increased vagal tone is a named cause in well-conditioned people.
Mobitz type II block
Mobitz type II drops beats without warning while the PR interval stays constant. Here the PR lengthens before each drop.

set1.q: A 66-year-old woman learns her electrocardiogram shows a constant PR interval of 0.22 seconds with every beat conducted. She feels well and asks at what point this kind of delay usually starts to cause symptoms. Which answer is most accurate?
opts: Once the PR exceeds 0.20 seconds
A PR over 0.20 seconds defines first-degree block, which she already has, yet most such patients feel nothing. Symptoms usually begin above 0.3 seconds.
Once the PR exceeds 0.12 seconds
A PR of 0.12 to 0.20 seconds is normal. Symptoms of first-degree block usually begin when the PR is over 0.3 seconds.
Only if a QRS starts dropping
Dropped beats would mean second-degree block, a different rhythm. Symptoms of first-degree block usually appear once the PR exceeds 0.3 seconds.
Once the PR exceeds 0.3 seconds
Correct. The vast majority of first-degree blocks are asymptomatic; symptoms such as fatigue, dyspnea, palpitations and chest pain usually appear once the PR interval is greater than 0.3 seconds.

set1.q: A 65-year-old man with a heart rate of 48 on metoprolol develops torsades de pointes (QRS complexes that twist around the baseline) from a drug-induced long QT. Which of his medications worsens this rhythm through an indirect effect on the QT?
opts: Aspirin
Aspirin has no named effect on the QT. Metoprolol indirectly prolongs it through bradycardia.
Lisinopril
Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors are not named. Metoprolol worsens torsades by slowing the rate.
Metoprolol
Correct. Beta blockers are avoided in torsades because the bradycardia they cause lengthens the R to R interval and so indirectly prolongs the QT.
Atorvastatin
Statins are not named for this. The beta blocker, by slowing the rate, indirectly prolongs the QT.

set1.q: A 67-year-old woman is in sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia at 150 per minute. Her blood pressure is 124/76 and she is alert, but she reports new chest pain. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Intravenous amiodarone
An antiarrhythmic is for the stable patient. Chest pain alone makes her unstable, which calls for synchronized cardioversion.
Defibrillation
Defibrillation is for the pulseless patient or polymorphic rhythm. She has a pulse and a monomorphic rhythm.
Observation and labs
Chest pain makes her unstable; waiting is unsafe. She needs synchronized cardioversion.
Synchronized cardioversion

Correct. Instability is defined by any one of chest pain, altered mental status, shortness of breath or hypotension; with chest pain and a pulse, she gets synchronized cardioversion despite a normal blood pressure.

set1.q: A 45-year-old man has a 24-hour monitor for an unrelated reason. It shows premature ventricular contractions in under 1% of beats. He has no symptoms, and his echocardiogram is normal. Which plan is most appropriate?
opts: Reassurance, remove triggers
Correct. Low-risk adults with a low burden (under 1% or 1,000 a day), no structural heart disease and no symptoms need reassurance and elimination of triggers.
Daily beta blocker
A beta blocker is first-line only for symptomatic low-risk patients. He has no symptoms, so reassurance is enough.
Catheter ablation
Ablation is kept for refractory symptoms or beat-induced cardiomyopathy, not a silent low burden.
Implantable defibrillator
A defibrillator prevents sudden death from lethal rhythms; rare benign premature beats need only reassurance.

set1.q: A 70-year-old woman with known complete heart block awaiting device placement reports two fainting episodes this week. Why is this symptom especially concerning?
opts: It suggests low blood glucose
Nothing points to hypoglycemia. Syncope in complete heart block is associated with an increased risk of sudden death.
It signals higher sudden death risk
Correct. Syncope is a particularly important symptom in complete heart block because it is associated with an increased risk of sudden death.
It means the block is resolving
Fainting does not mean recovery. In complete block, syncope is associated with an increased risk of sudden death.
It points to a seizure disorder
Her collapse is explained by the slow escape rhythm. Syncope in complete block signals an increased risk of sudden death.

set1.q: A 69-year-old woman in a regular wide QRS tachycardia with identical complexes suddenly becomes unresponsive, and no pulse can be felt. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Intravenous lidocaine
A drug alone is for the stable patient. Pulseless ventricular tachycardia is defibrillated.
Vagal maneuvers
Vagal maneuvers act on the atrioventricular node in supraventricular rhythms; they have no role in pulseless ventricular tachycardia.
Defibrillation
Correct. Pulseless ventricular tachycardia is treated with defibrillation (unsynchronized cardioversion) and cardiopulmonary resuscitation, the same steps as ventricular fibrillation.
Synchronized cardioversion
Synchronized cardioversion is for unstable ventricular tachycardia with a pulse. Without a pulse, defibrillate.

set1.q: A 74-year-old woman with no symptoms and normal exercise tolerance has a routine electrocardiogram showing a constant PR interval of 0.24 seconds, with every P wave conducted to a narrow QRS complex. Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Transcutaneous pacing
Transcutaneous pacing is the emergency bridge for unstable Mobitz type II or complete block, not for a stable, silent first-degree block.
Oral beta blocker
A beta blocker slows atrioventricular conduction and is itself a named cause of first-degree block; it would not treat it.
No treatment needed
Correct. Asymptomatic first-degree atrioventricular block needs no treatment; a permanent pacemaker is considered only if debilitating symptoms or heart failure symptoms develop.
Permanent pacemaker
A pacemaker is considered for symptomatic first-degree block. A symptom-free older adult with a PR of 0.24 seconds needs no treatment.

set1.q: A 61-year-old man with a long QT has recurrent runs of torsades de pointes (QRS complexes that twist around the baseline). Between runs he is alert, with a pulse and a normal blood pressure. Which is the first treatment?
opts: Intravenous amiodarone
Amiodarone prolongs the QT and is avoided in torsades. Intravenous magnesium comes first.
Intravenous procainamide
Procainamide prolongs the QT and is avoided in torsades. Magnesium is the first treatment.
Intravenous metoprolol
Beta blockers are avoided because the slower rate indirectly lengthens the QT. Magnesium is given first.
Intravenous magnesium
Correct. In a conscious patient, intravenous magnesium breaks torsades, followed by more magnesium as an infusion.

set1.q: A 38-year-old man who injects drugs is being treated for aortic valve endocarditis. On day 4 his heart rate falls to 38, and the electrocardiogram shows P waves with no relationship to wide QRS complexes. Which complication of his infection explains the new rhythm?
opts: Drug-induced vagal tone
Increased vagal tone causes milder nodal blocks. Complete block during endocarditis points to an abscess.
A perivalvular abscess
Correct. Bacterial endocarditis with an associated abscess is a named cause of complete heart block, because the infection extends into the conduction tissue.
Septic emboli to the lungs
Septic pulmonary emboli cause cough and lung lesions, not heart block. An abscess near the conduction system does.
Splinter hemorrhages
Splinter hemorrhages are nail-bed signs of endocarditis and do not affect conduction. An abscess is the cause of the block.

set1.q: An 84-year-old woman with no heart symptoms has a right bundle branch block on a routine electrocardiogram. She has no lung disease, no recent immobility and a normal echocardiogram. Which named cause best fits her?
opts: Pulmonary hypertension
Pulmonary hypertension is a named cause, but she has no lung disease and a normal echocardiogram. Age-related degeneration fits.
Age-related degeneration
Correct. Age-related degenerative change of the conduction system heads the list of causes of right bundle branch block and best fits an elderly patient with no other disease.
Pulmonary embolism
A pulmonary embolism causes an acute right bundle branch block with sudden dyspnea. She has no symptoms or risk factors for it.
Myocarditis
Myocarditis is an inflammatory cause with symptoms and an abnormal heart. Her silent block fits age-related degeneration.

set1.q: A 52-year-old man has a cardiac arrest after choking on food at a restaurant. The obstruction is removed, but he remains pulseless with an organized rhythm on the monitor. Compressions are underway. Which airway step should be considered early?
opts: A nebulized bronchodilator
A bronchodilator does not secure the airway. Early intubation addresses his hypoxia.
Intubation
Correct. Pulseless electrical activity is unshockable; compressions start at once and intubation is considered early, since hypoxia is one of its two leading causes.
Defibrillation first
An organized pulseless rhythm is unshockable. Early intubation addresses the hypoxia that caused it.
Wait for a pulse first
Airway support is not delayed until a pulse returns; intubation is considered early.

set1.q: A 66-year-old woman with chronic obstructive lung disease is admitted with an exacerbation. She is confused, and the monitor shows runs of skipped beats from frequent early, wide QRS complexes without P waves. Her arterial oxygen tension is low. Which underlying problem should be corrected first?
opts: Her blood pressure
Blood pressure is not the named trigger. Hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalance are the main causes of premature ventricular contractions.
Her blood glucose
Blood glucose is not a named trigger. Her low oxygen tension is the cause to correct first.
Her body temperature
Temperature is not the named trigger. Hypoxemia, with electrolyte imbalance, drives premature ventricular contractions.
Her hypoxemia
Correct. Hypoxemia is a main cause of premature ventricular contractions, along with electrolyte imbalance, so her low oxygen should be corrected first.

set1.q: A 78-year-old woman has a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids, and her electrocardiogram shows a left bundle branch block. Which of her conditions is singled out as a cause of this block?
opts: Mitral stenosis
Mitral stenosis gives a diastolic rumble at the apex, not this murmur, and is not singled out. Aortic stenosis is.
Pulmonic stenosis
Pulmonic stenosis loads the right ventricle and is heard at the left upper sternal border. Aortic stenosis is the lesion named.
Tricuspid regurgitation
Tricuspid regurgitation is a right-sided holosystolic murmur. The valve lesion singled out for left bundle branch block is aortic stenosis.
Aortic stenosis
Correct. Valvular heart disease, especially aortic stenosis, is a named cause of left bundle branch block, and her murmur is the classic aortic stenosis murmur.

set1.q: A 75-year-old man with complete heart block is stabilized with transcutaneous pacing in the emergency department. Which is the definitive treatment?
opts: Oral beta blocker
A beta blocker slows conduction further. Complete block is treated definitively with a permanent pacemaker.
Permanent pacemaker
Correct. Transcutaneous pacing is the emergent bridge; the definitive treatment for complete (third-degree) atrioventricular block is a permanent pacemaker.
Implantable defibrillator
An implantable cardioverter defibrillator shocks lethal ventricular rhythms. Complete block needs a permanent pacemaker.
Catheter ablation
Ablation destroys conduction tissue and is itself a named cause of complete block. The definitive treatment is a permanent pacemaker.

set1.q: A 34-year-old man is brought in after a motorcycle crash with a large thigh wound and heavy blood loss. He has no pulse. The monitor shows a regular narrow-complex rhythm at 110 per minute. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Sinus tachycardia
Sinus tachycardia has a pulse. Without a pulse, the same organized rhythm is pulseless electrical activity.
Pulseless electrical activity
Correct. An organized rhythm on which a pulse would be expected, but with no pulse, is pulseless electrical activity; hypovolemia is one of its two leading causes in adults.
Ventricular fibrillation
Fibrillation is chaotic with no organized complexes. A regular narrow rhythm without a pulse is pulseless electrical activity.
Asystole
Asystole is a flat line. This monitor shows an organized rhythm, so it is pulseless electrical activity.

set1.q: A 41-year-old woman with symptomatic premature ventricular contractions and a structurally normal heart stopped her beta blocker after two weeks because of fatigue and dizziness. Her symptoms persist. Which is the most appropriate next option?
opts: Permanent pacemaker
A pacemaker treats slow conduction. Drug-intolerant symptomatic premature beats are treated with catheter ablation.
Reassurance only
Reassurance alone fits silent, low-burden beats. She has persistent symptoms and cannot take a beta blocker, so ablation is next.
Catheter ablation
Correct. In low-risk symptomatic patients, a beta blocker is first-line, and catheter ablation is used if symptoms are refractory or the patient cannot tolerate drug therapy.
Implantable defibrillator
A defibrillator prevents sudden death from lethal rhythms; it does not treat premature beats. Ablation is the next option.

Correct. A new right bundle branch block is not always pathological; it may occur in people with no apparent underlying heart disease, and treatment depends on any underlying condition.
It proves a past heart attack
A right bundle branch block does not prove an old infarction. It may occur with no apparent underlying heart disease.
It requires a pacemaker
An isolated right bundle branch block does not need pacing; treatment depends on the underlying condition.
It always becomes complete block
Isolated right bundle branch block does not inevitably progress to complete block. It may occur with no apparent heart disease.

set1.q: A 77-year-old woman with known Mobitz type II block suddenly collapses while gardening and regains consciousness within a minute; her husband saw brief jerking of her arms. Her heart rate is 36. Which term describes this event?
opts: Stokes-Adams attack
Correct. A Stokes-Adams attack is a sudden fainting spell or seizure from a rapid, temporary drop in blood flow to the brain, a recognized complication of Mobitz type II block.
Vasovagal syncope
Vasovagal syncope follows a trigger such as pain or standing, with a prodrome. A sudden faint from a blocked rhythm with a rate of 36 is a Stokes-Adams attack.
Absence seizure
An absence seizure is a brief staring spell without collapse. Her collapse came from low cerebral blood flow during heart block.
Transient ischemic attack
A transient ischemic attack causes focal neurologic deficits, not a sudden faint with a slow rate. This is a Stokes-Adams attack.

set1.q: A 64-year-old man with crushing chest pain develops a wide QRS tachycardia whose complexes vary in shape from beat to beat; his QT before the episode was normal. He is still talking and has a pulse. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Defibrillation
Correct. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never truly stable, only a short-lived transitional state, so it is defibrillated even when the patient has a pulse and looks well.
Synchronized cardioversion
Synchronized cardioversion needs a consistent QRS; it suits unstable monomorphic rhythm. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is defibrillated.
Intravenous amiodarone alone
Drug therapy alone is for stable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia needs defibrillation.
Observation on the monitor
Watching is unsafe: polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is never stable and is defibrillated.

opts: Ablation is a named cause of it
Correct. Cardiac ablation is listed among the causes of Mobitz type I block, along with increased vagal tone, nodal blocking drugs, Lyme carditis and ischemia after infarction.
It proves the ablation failed
A new conduction delay does not mean the original tachycardia remains. Ablation itself is a named cause of Mobitz type I block.
It signals acute Lyme carditis
Lyme carditis is a cause, but nothing here suggests tick exposure. The recent ablation is the named cause that fits.
It must progress to complete block
Mobitz type I is usually benign; it is Mobitz type II that carries a high risk of complete block. Ablation is a named cause.

set2.q: A 72-year-old man with congestive heart failure and an ejection fraction of 20% is in stable, sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with a pulse. Which intravenous antiarrhythmic should be avoided?
opts: Amiodarone
Amiodarone is a named option for stable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia. The drug to avoid in heart failure is procainamide.
Magnesium

Procainamide
Correct. Procainamide should be avoided in a prolonged QT or congestive heart failure; lidocaine or amiodarone are the other named options for stable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia.
Lidocaine
Lidocaine is one of the named drugs for stable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia and carries no heart failure caution here. Procainamide does.

set2.q: An 81-year-old man takes no medications and has never had a heart attack. A routine electrocardiogram shows a constant PR interval of 0.25 seconds with every beat conducted, and he asks why his heart is doing this. Which explanation is most accurate?
opts: An overactive vagus nerve
Increased vagal tone is a named cause, typically in young, well-conditioned people. In an 81-year-old, age-related degeneration is the usual cause.
Age-related wear of the pathway
Correct. The most common cause of first-degree atrioventricular block is age-related degenerative change of the conduction system, so the impulse takes longer to cross the atrioventricular node.
A silent tick-borne infection
Lyme carditis is a named cause, but without exposure or a rash the leading explanation in an older man is degeneration of the conduction system.
Hidden damage from a heart attack
Atrioventricular node ischemia usually follows a myocardial infarction, which he has never had. Age-related degeneration is the most common cause.

opts: Coronary disease is the top risk
Correct. Coronary artery disease is the most common predisposing condition for sudden cardiac death, even in adults without a history of myocardial infarction.
Risk starts only after an infarction
Coronary artery disease predisposes to sudden death even without a prior myocardial infarction.
Only inherited rhythms raise risk
Inherited conditions such as long QT syndrome exist, but coronary artery disease is the most common predisposing condition.
Risk applies only after age 80
No age cutoff is stated. Coronary artery disease is the most common predisposing condition for sudden cardiac death.

set2.q: A 27-year-old graduate student drinks several energy drinks a day and has occasional skipped beats. A monitor shows isolated premature ventricular contractions; his echocardiogram and electrolytes are normal. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
opts: Start lifelong amiodarone
Amiodarone is for ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation and has many side effects. Removing caffeine and stimulants is the advice here.
Cut caffeine and stimulants
Correct. Alcohol, caffeine and stimulants are named triggers of premature ventricular contractions, and low-risk patients are reassured and helped to eliminate triggers.
Avoid all exercise
Exercise is not a named trigger to remove. Caffeine and stimulants, such as energy drinks, are.
Avoid dairy products
Dairy foods are not a named trigger of premature beats. Caffeine, stimulants and alcohol are the named triggers.

set2.q: A 72-year-old man has fatigue, shortness of breath on exertion and palpitations. His electrocardiogram shows every P wave conducted to a narrow QRS with a constant PR interval of 0.34 seconds. No offending drug or reversible cause is found. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Intravenous magnesium
Magnesium is the treatment for torsades de pointes. Symptomatic first-degree block with a PR over 0.3 seconds is managed with a pacemaker.
Permanent pacemaker
Correct. First-degree block causes symptoms once the PR interval exceeds 0.3 seconds, and a permanent pacemaker is considered for symptomatic patients when no reversible cause is found.
Reassurance only
Reassurance fits the asymptomatic patient. Symptoms with a PR above 0.3 seconds make him a candidate for a permanent pacemaker.
Synchronized cardioversion
Cardioversion terminates tachycardias. A long PR interval with a normal rate is a conduction delay, which is paced, not shocked.

His electrocardiogram shows a constant PR interval of 0.30 seconds with every P wave conducted. Which infection should be suspected as the cause of his conduction delay?
opts: Viral pharyngitis
A sore-throat virus is not a named cause of atrioventricular block. The tick bite and rash point to Lyme carditis.
Lyme disease
Correct. Lyme disease (Lyme carditis) is a named infectious cause of atrioventricular block at every degree, and a tick bite with an expanding rash points to it.
Infective endocarditis
Endocarditis causes block through an abscess near the conduction system, usually with fever and a murmur. A tick bite with an expanding rash points to Lyme disease.
Chagas disease
Chagas disease causes complete block in people from areas where it is endemic. A tick bite in New England with an expanding rash points to Lyme disease.

opts: Defibrillation
Defibrillation is for the pulseless patient. He still has a pulse, so the shock is synchronized.
Intravenous amiodarone
Drugs alone are for the stable patient. Confusion and hypotension call for synchronized cardioversion.
Transcutaneous pacing
Pacing treats slow, blocked rhythms. A fast, unstable ventricular tachycardia with a pulse is cardioverted.
Synchronized cardioversion
Correct. Altered mental status and hypotension define instability; with a pulse still present, unstable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia is treated with synchronized cardioversion.

set2.q: A 55-year-old woman taking a loop diuretic for heart failure has new palpitations felt in her neck. Telemetry shows frequent premature ventricular contractions. Which laboratory values should be checked first?
opts: Potassium and magnesium
Correct. Electrolyte imbalances, especially hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia (with hypercalcemia), are main causes of premature ventricular contractions, and a loop diuretic can lower both.
Thyroid hormone, cortisol
Thyroid and adrenal tests are not the first step. Premature ventricular contractions call for potassium and magnesium levels.
Troponin and lipase
These look for infarction and pancreatitis. Frequent premature beats on a diuretic call for potassium and magnesium.
Glucose and lactate
Glucose and lactate are not the named triggers. Low potassium and low magnesium are.

Magnesium treats torsades de pointes. Asystole is treated with compressions and epinephrine.
Epinephrine
Correct. High-quality chest compressions and epinephrine by intravenous or intraosseous push at intervals are the mainstays of treatment for asystole.
Amiodarone
Amiodarone is for shock-refractory ventricular fibrillation or tachycardia. Asystole relies on compressions and epinephrine.

Lidocaine is considered in shock-refractory fibrillation. Asystole is treated with compressions and epinephrine.

The electrocardiogram shows regular P waves at 80 per minute and regular wide QRS complexes at 36 per minute, with no consistent relationship between them; some P waves sit inside T waves. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Complete heart block
Correct. Two separate regular rhythms, with atria faster than the ventricles and P waves falling anywhere (even within T waves), is third-degree (complete) atrioventricular block.
Mobitz type II block
Mobitz type II conducts most P waves at a constant PR and drops some. Here no P wave relates to any QRS.
Mobitz type I block
Mobitz type I shows a PR that lengthens until a drop. Here there is no consistent PR at all.
Ventricular tachycardia
Ventricular tachycardia is a fast wide rhythm of 100 to 250 per minute. A wide rhythm at 36 with dissociated P waves is complete block.

opts: Implantable loop recorder
A loop recorder only records the rhythm. He needs a device that detects and shocks lethal rhythms.
Biventricular pacemaker
A biventricular pacer treats symptomatic left bundle branch block with reduced ejection fraction. Arrest survivors need a defibrillator.
Implantable defibrillator
Correct. Once stabilized after life-threatening ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation, most patients need an implantable cardioverter defibrillator for secondary prevention of sudden cardiac death.
Permanent pacemaker
A pacemaker treats slow, blocked rhythms. Survivors of ventricular tachycardia arrest need a defibrillator.

opts: Treat any underlying condition
Correct. Right bundle branch block is usually asymptomatic, and its treatment depends on the underlying condition; prognosis depends on the presence and type of heart disease.
Permanent pacemaker
A pacemaker is not indicated for an isolated, silent right bundle branch block. Treatment targets any underlying condition.
Biventricular pacemaker
A biventricular pacer is used for symptomatic left bundle branch block with reduced ejection fraction, not a silent right bundle branch block.
Catheter ablation
Ablation cannot fix a bundle branch block. Treatment depends on the underlying condition.

opts: Better than fibrillation
Ventricular fibrillation has a better prognosis than asystole. Asystole is usually an end-of-life rhythm.
Recovery is expected
Recovery is not expected; asystole carries a poor prognosis and is usually an end-of-life rhythm.
Prognosis is poor
Correct. Asystole and pulseless electrical activity carry a poor prognosis and are usually end-of-life rhythms; ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation have the best prognosis.
A shock should restore it
Asystole is unshockable; there is no electrical activity to reset. Its prognosis is poor.

opts: Catheter ablation
Correct. Isolated premature ventricular contraction-induced cardiomyopathy with heart failure signs and symptoms, in a high-risk patient with a burden over 15%, is treated with catheter ablation.
Reassurance only
Reassurance is for low-burden, symptom-free patients with normal hearts. His beats have caused a cardiomyopathy.
Digoxin
Digoxin is not named for this. Premature ventricular contraction-induced cardiomyopathy is treated with catheter ablation.
Intravenous magnesium
Magnesium is the treatment for torsades de pointes. Beat-induced cardiomyopathy is treated with catheter ablation.

opts: Detect and shock fatal rhythms
Correct. The implantable cardioverter defibrillator prevents sudden cardiac death: sensing electrodes detect fatal arrhythmias and the device delivers a shock, and newer models can also pace.
Slowly dissolve artery plaque
No device dissolves plaque. The defibrillator senses fatal arrhythmias and delivers a shock.
Only record her rhythm
A recorder only stores the rhythm. The defibrillator detects fatal arrhythmias and treats them with a shock.
Replace her heart medications
The device does not replace medical therapy. It detects fatal arrhythmias and delivers a shock.

opts: Conduction system wear
Correct. The most common cause of Mobitz type II is acquired disease of the His-Purkinje system, especially degenerative change from old age, chronic hypertension and diabetes.
An overactive vagus nerve
Increased vagal tone causes first-degree and Mobitz type I block, usually in younger, fit people. Mobitz type II comes from His-Purkinje disease.
His blood pressure tablets
He takes no rate-slowing drugs. His long-standing hypertension and diabetes drive degenerative His-Purkinje disease, the most common cause.
A recent viral illness
He has had no infections. The leading cause of Mobitz type II is degenerative His-Purkinje disease, driven by age, hypertension and diabetes.

opts: It is caused by vagal tone
Increased vagal tone causes milder blocks at the node, not complete block with syncope. Infiltrative sarcoidosis is a named cause.
It will resolve without treatment
Complete block with syncope carries an increased risk of sudden death and needs pacing; it should not be expected to resolve.
It is a drug side effect
Nothing in her history points to a drug. Sarcoidosis, an infiltrative disease, is a named cause of complete block.
Sarcoidosis is a named cause
Correct. Inflammatory and infiltrative disease, namely myocarditis, amyloidosis and sarcoidosis, is a named cause of complete heart block.

Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion
Synchronized cardioversion treats unstable tachycardias with a pulse. A slow rate from a failing conduction system needs pacing.
Defibrillation
Defibrillation is for ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia. She has a pulse and a slow, blocked rhythm.
Observation on a monitor
Observation is unsafe with hypotension and confusion. Unstable Mobitz type II block is paced transcutaneously.
Transcutaneous pacing
Correct. When medications are not used or do not work in unstable Mobitz type II block, the emergent measure is transcutaneous pacing, which bridges her to a permanent pacemaker.

Adenosine
Adenosine is for narrow-complex supraventricular tachycardia. Lidocaine is considered here.
Lidocaine
Correct. Lidocaine is considered for ventricular fibrillation that remains refractory to shocks after amiodarone.
Verapamil
Verapamil is a nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker for atrial rhythms. Lidocaine may be considered in shock-refractory arrest.

opts: Tuberculosis
Tuberculosis is not on the list of causes of complete block. Chagas disease, endemic in Latin America, is.
Chagas disease
Correct. Chagas disease is a named cause of complete heart block; it is a parasitic infection endemic in parts of Latin America such as rural Bolivia.
Lyme disease
Lyme carditis is a named cause of block, but it follows a tick bite in endemic areas such as New England. His background points to Chagas disease.
Malaria
Malaria is not a named cause of complete block. A man from rural Bolivia with complete block suggests Chagas disease.

Amiodarone
Correct. If ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia persists after shocks, amiodarone is given by rapid intravenous or intraosseous push.
Adenosine
Adenosine is for narrow-complex supraventricular tachycardia. Shock-refractory fibrillation gets amiodarone.
Diltiazem
Diltiazem slows atrioventricular conduction in atrial rhythms. Shock-refractory fibrillation gets amiodarone.

set2.q: A 69-year-old woman with a long-standing left bundle branch block now has dizziness, shortness of breath and dyspnea on exertion that resemble a heart failure flare. What does the onset of symptoms from the block usually indicate?
opts: Accessory pathway
An accessory pathway causes pre-excitation. Symptoms in left bundle branch block point to severe underlying heart disease.
Severe heart disease
Correct. Most patients with left bundle branch block are asymptomatic; those who develop symptoms usually have severe underlying cardiac disease and do not tolerate the block well.
A harmless variant
A harmless variant would not cause these symptoms. Symptomatic left bundle branch block points to severe underlying heart disease.
A drug side effect
Nothing suggests a drug cause. Symptoms from the block usually mean severe underlying cardiac disease.

set2.q: A 58-year-old man on telemetry has an 18-second run of identical wide QRS complexes at 180 per minute. During the run his blood pressure falls to 70/40 and he nearly faints; the run then stops on its own. How should this episode be classified?
opts: Ventricular fibrillation
Fibrillation is disorganized activity with no pulse. Identical wide complexes at a regular rate are ventricular tachycardia.
Ventricular bigeminy
Bigeminy alternates normal and ectopic beats. A continuous run of wide complexes is ventricular tachycardia.
Sustained ventricular tachycardia
Correct. Ventricular tachycardia counts as sustained if it lasts 30 seconds or more or causes hemodynamic collapse in under 30 seconds; his hypotension makes an 18-second run sustained.
Non-sustained ventricular tachycardia
Under 30 seconds is non-sustained only if the patient stays stable. Hypotension and near-fainting make this run sustained.

set2.q: A 70-year-old woman with ischemic cardiomyopathy has had a regular wide QRS tachycardia at 160 per minute, with identical complexes, for 10 minutes. She is alert and talking, her blood pressure is 118/74, and she has no chest pain or shortness of breath. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Immediate defibrillation
Defibrillation is for pulseless or polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. A stable monomorphic rhythm with a pulse is treated with drugs first.
Synchronized cardioversion
Synchronized cardioversion is for instability: chest pain, altered mental status, dyspnea or hypotension. She has none of these.
Intravenous adenosine
Adenosine acts on the atrioventricular node in supraventricular rhythms. Stable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia gets an intravenous antiarrhythmic.
Intravenous antiarrhythmic

Correct. Hemodynamically stable, monomorphic sustained ventricular tachycardia is pharmacologically cardioverted with intravenous lidocaine, amiodarone or procainamide, with monitoring, intravenous access, a 12-lead electrocardiogram, oxygen and labs.

set2.q: A 70-year-old woman on telemetry has torsades de pointes (QRS complexes that twist around the baseline). An intravenous push of magnesium broke the first run, but short runs keep recurring. She is alert with a pulse and a normal blood pressure. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Intravenous procainamide
Procainamide prolongs the QT and is avoided in torsades. A magnesium infusion follows the first push.
Synchronized cardioversion
She is stable, and a polymorphic rhythm cannot be synchronized. Recurrent runs get a magnesium infusion.
Magnesium infusion
Correct. Torsades in a conscious patient is broken with intravenous magnesium and then treated with more magnesium as an infusion: magnesium, and more magnesium.
Intravenous amiodarone
Amiodarone prolongs the QT and is avoided in torsades. Recurrent runs are treated with a magnesium infusion.

set2.q: A 52-year-old man on telemetry has a prolonged QT after starting a new medication and then develops polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (QRS complexes that vary in shape and twist around the baseline). He becomes unresponsive and pulseless. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion
Synchronized shocks need a consistent QRS and a pulse. Pulseless polymorphic tachycardia is defibrillated.
Intravenous magnesium only
Magnesium breaks torsades in a conscious patient; a pulseless patient needs defibrillation first.
Transcutaneous pacing
Pacing treats slow, blocked rhythms. A pulseless polymorphic tachycardia is defibrillated.
Defibrillation
Correct. Pulseless polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, including torsades, is treated as cardiac arrest with defibrillation and cardiopulmonary resuscitation; magnesium follows.

set2.q: A 70-year-old man with hypertension is told that a routine electrocardiogram shows a long-standing left bundle branch block, unchanged from tracings years ago. He feels well and has a normal ejection fraction. He asks whether it needs treatment. Which answer is most accurate?
opts: He needs a pacemaker now
A pacemaker is not indicated for a stable, silent left bundle branch block with a normal ejection fraction.
He needs a defibrillator
A defibrillator prevents sudden death from lethal ventricular rhythms; it is not a treatment for a silent bundle branch block.
He needs catheter ablation
Ablation cannot fix a bundle branch block. A silent, long-standing left bundle branch block is usually left untreated.
It is usually left untreated
Correct. Left bundle branch block is usually left untreated; the exception is symptomatic left bundle branch block with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, which gets a biventricular pacer.

set2.q: A 47-year-old woman with five days of vomiting and diarrhea has a prolonged QT and brief runs of torsades de pointes (QRS complexes that twist around the baseline). Which electrolyte disturbances should be sought as causes of her long QT?
opts: High potassium, high calcium
High potassium and high calcium are not named; hypercalcemia actually shortens the QT. Low potassium and low calcium prolong it.
Low sodium, high chloride
Sodium and chloride are not the named disturbances. Hypokalemia and hypocalcemia are.
High sodium, low phosphate
These are not the named causes of a long QT. Low potassium and low calcium prolong it.
Low potassium, low calcium
Correct. Besides drugs, hypokalemia and hypocalcemia are named causes of acquired long QT syndrome, which underlies most torsades de pointes.

set2.q: A 62-year-old woman taking metoprolol and diltiazem for palpitations has a new rhythm in which the PR interval lengthens until a QRS is dropped. She has mild fatigue. Which part of her history is a named cause of this rhythm?
opts: Her mild fatigue
Fatigue is a possible symptom of the block, not its cause. Her rate-slowing medications are the named cause.
Her female sex
Sex is not a named cause. Beta blockers and nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are listed causes of Mobitz type I.
Her rate-slowing drugs
Correct. Beta blockers and nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, with digoxin, are named causes of Mobitz type I block, so her medication list is the first place to look.
Her history of palpitations
Palpitations are the reason for her drugs, not a cause of block. Her beta blocker and nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker are named causes.

set2.q: A 58-year-old woman five days after hip replacement develops sudden breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain and a heart rate of 118. Her electrocardiogram shows a new right bundle branch block. Which acute cause of the block should be suspected?
opts: Pulmonary embolism
Correct. A sudden increase in right ventricular pressure, as from a pulmonary embolism, is a named cause of right bundle branch block, and her postoperative setting fits.
Aortic dissection
Aortic dissection causes tearing chest or back pain and loads the aorta, not the right ventricle. Pulmonary embolism fits her picture.
Pericardial effusion
An effusion lowers voltage and can cause tamponade, but it is not the named acute cause of right bundle branch block. Pulmonary embolism is.
Hypertensive crisis
A hypertensive crisis loads the left ventricle. A sudden right ventricular pressure rise from pulmonary embolism fits.
